title: Frigaliment Importing Co., Ltd. v. B.N.S. International Sales Corp.
lead: A Swiss buyer expected young broiling birds, a New York seller supplied stewing chickens, and the trial judge had to decide whether the buyer proved that their contracts used “chicken” in its narrower sense.

actors.name: B.N.S. International Sales Corp.
actors.role: New York seller, new to the poultry trade in 1957

actors.name: Ernest Bauer
actors.role: B.N.S. secretary who negotiated the orders

actors.name: Stovicek
actors.role: Intermediary who presented Frigaliment’s cables and discussed their meaning

actors.name: Judge Henry Friendly
actors.role: Circuit judge deciding the trial action in district court

proceedings: Buyer sued for breach of the statutory warranty that goods match their description; Judge Friendly made trial findings and directed judgment dismissing the complaint with costs on December 27, 1960.
limits: This was a trial decision under the law the parties agreed was New York law. The judgment reflects the buyer’s failure of proof, not a universal definition of chicken or a determination of bad faith.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with complete effective canonical brief; no new independent full-opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Two export orders met an unexpected shipment
sections.cue: Start with the promised goods, prices, and discovery.
paragraphs: Frigaliment Importing Co., a Swiss corporation, sought poultry through an April 26, 1957 cable shown to B.N.S. International Sales Corp., a New York seller, during negotiations in New York. The companies made two contracts on May 2. The first order called for 75,000 pounds of birds weighing 2½–3 pounds at $33 per hundredweight and 25,000 pounds weighing 1½–2 pounds at $36.50 per hundredweight. The description specified fresh-frozen, Grade A, government-inspected, eviscerated U.S. chicken, individually Cryovac-wrapped and export-packed, for May 10 shipment free alongside ship in New York. A second contract reduced the heavier quantity to 50,000 pounds, priced the smaller birds at $37 per hundredweight, and scheduled May 30 shipment.

The first shipment was short, and its balance went out May 17. After the poultry reached Switzerland, Frigaliment discovered on May 28 that the heavier birds were mature stewing chickens. Many packages identified them as such. Frigaliment protested that it had bought young broilers or fryers. A second shipment nevertheless left May 29 with mature heavier birds again, and B.N.S. stopped its transportation at Rotterdam.

Frigaliment sued for breach of the statutory warranty that goods correspond to their description. B.N.S. maintained that any chickens meeting the specified grade and weights satisfied the contracts. Circuit Judge Henry Friendly decided the action as a trial judge in the district court. He applied New York law because the parties apparently agreed it governed despite acceptance in Switzerland. Their failure to invoke a Produce Exchange arbitration clause was treated as agreement to eliminate that remedy.

sections.title: The bargaining conversation complicated the buyer’s reading
sections.cue: Introduce the negotiators and explain the contested evidence.
paragraphs: The word “chicken” had both broad and narrow dictionary meanings. Frigaliment argued that the smaller birds necessarily were young, so the common description restricted the heavier birds as well. Friendly found that unpersuasive: a general commodity description could encompass different varieties in different sizes. The government-inspection and grading terms could also support the seller’s reading.

The negotiations had occurred in New York between Ernest Bauer, B.N.S.’s secretary, and Stovicek, who was visiting for the Czechoslovak government at the World Trade Fair. Stovicek showed Bauer Frigaliment’s April 26 cable seeking heavier chickens at no more than 33 cents per pound. Bauer checked prices and accepted; later cables added quantities. Frigaliment emphasized that the mainly German cables retained the English word “chicken,” although the general German term included both broilers and stewing birds. It argued that B.N.S.’s German-speaking officers should have understood that choice to narrow the order.

Bauer testified, however, that he asked what kind of chickens were wanted and was told any kind. He said he then specifically confirmed that the cable meant the broader German term. Friendly found no inconsistency of the kind Frigaliment alleged between Bauer’s testimony and deposition. Nor could Frigaliment rely on its cable as a definition while rejecting the explanatory response of the intermediary entrusted with it. Even if Stovicek could not change prices or dates, he had that interpretive role. A blank intermediary line on the forms concerned the commission recipient and did not erase his participation.

sections.title: Competing trade evidence failed to establish a universal usage
sections.cue: Show why the seller’s newcomer status changed the buyer’s proof.
paragraphs: B.N.S. had entered the poultry trade only in 1957. To bind a newcomer to a trade usage, Frigaliment needed to show actual knowledge or a sufficiently longstanding, notorious, universal, and reasonable practice to charge the seller with knowledge. Actual knowledge of the alleged narrow usage was not proved; B.N.S. believed the contrary.

Frigaliment offered testimony from Strasser, a buyer for Swiss cooperatives; Niesielowski, an officer of a supplier; and Dates of the Urner-Barry reporting service. Publications also distinguished young chicken from fowl. Yet Strasser used explicit broiler or fowl terminology in his own purchases. Niesielowski responded to an inquiry for chickens by asking which class was wanted, ultimately supplied fowl, and later asked for a confirmation using stewing-chicken terminology. Those practices weakened the claim that “chicken” alone universally meant a young bird.

B.N.S.’s witnesses Weininger, Fox, and Sadina supported the inclusive meaning. Government purchasing specifications included mature birds; industry statistics divided chicken into young and mature categories; Agriculture Department reports specified classes instead of relying on the unqualified word. The conflict prevented Frigaliment from proving the binding usage it alleged. Friendly did not declare trade usage irrelevant or hold that lack of actual knowledge always defeats it.

sections.title: Regulations and prices supported one reading; later conduct did not settle it
sections.cue: Keep the court’s qualifications with the evidence they limit.
paragraphs: The Agriculture Department classification treated broilers, roasters, capons, stags, hens or stewing chickens or fowl, and old roosters as classes of chicken. Frigaliment answered that it had incorporated only inspection and grade and that the trade ignored the regulatory definition. Seller witnesses disputed that account. Friendly used the regulations as a contextual dictionary, particularly because government grading appeared in Frigaliment’s original cable. His conclusion rested on at least an indirect contractual reference, without requiring wholesale incorporation of every regulatory detail.

The 33-cent heavier-bird price also favored B.N.S.: broilers then cost 35–37 cents, whereas B.N.S. obtained fowl for 30 cents. Saying that 33 cents lay closer to the broiler price did not explain why the seller would intentionally accept a loss. Still, Friendly did not conclusively find that these market implications had been adequately communicated to Frigaliment.

B.N.S. also relied on Frigaliment’s allowing the second shipment after a cable distinguished chickens from broilers. Friendly gave that conduct no interpretive weight because Frigaliment continued to demand contractual performance and reserve responsibility for costs. It might affect a disputed New York-versus-European damages measure if liability existed. Nor did later European resale using poultry terminology make the buyer’s objection fabricated: Frigaliment had protested immediately and consistently. The cables were German with the important English poultry terms retained.

sections.title: The buyer bore a burden it did not carry
sections.cue: End with the exact trial judgment and its limited meaning.
paragraphs: B.N.S.’s broad understanding aligned with a dictionary meaning, regulatory classification, some trade evidence, prices, and the buyer’s intermediary’s response. Subjective belief alone would not have sufficed. Friendly did not have to decide whether Frigaliment actually intended only young birds: the buyer bore the burden of proving that the contracts used the narrower meaning, and the whole record did not establish it.

On December 27, 1960, Friendly directed judgment dismissing the complaint with costs. The buyer failed to establish its asserted warranty breach; the court neither announced a definition for all poultry contracts nor found either side acted in bad faith. There was no appellate panel, separate opinion, or remand.
